rising cost of living turned violent yesterday as protesters destroyed property and charred
streets and buildings in cities across the country. Empiers Eleanor Beardsley has more.
There was wide-scale looting, but other cultural heritage losses were even more devastating.
A 140-year-old town hall was largely destroyed in the central town of Limoges after massed
perpetrators set the building alight. Some 550,000 people took part in the nationwide protest that
initially began with students protesting the state of education. They now include workers angry about
the cost of living, inequalities, and a government they hate. The violence ignited due to several
reasons. Far-left troublemakers looking to fight with police, outside youths who showed up to loot
after stores were broken into, and weeks of overly aggressive police tactics that have left
many young protesters angry and on edge. Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
At least one person are dead. Five others are injured after Ukraine carried out a waves of
drone strikes in Russia. This, despite pressure from President Trump, to end those strikes.
It's one of the largest attacks in the war since Russia started more than four years ago.
Empiers Charles Maynes has more. According to Russia's regional governor,
Ukrainian drones struck a range of strategic targets in St. Petersburg,
including the city's port oil terminal and a refinery. The attacks follow a similar targeting
of a key oil facility that services the capital, Moscow, earlier this week. President Trump has
condemned Ukraine for resuming strikes on Russian oil facilities. That criticism, coming days after
Trump announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel fuel in an attempt to tamp down gas prices in the
U.S. ahead of midterm elections. Ukraine's president, Vladimir Zelensky, says he was forced
to abandon Trump's declared energy truce, noting Russia had never paused its attacks on Ukraine's
heating and electrical systems. Charles Maynes, NPR News, Moscow. The midterm elections are just
weeks away, but early voting is underway in many states, including North Carolina.
That's where hundreds of college students in Greensboro marched to the polls last week for
the first day of early voting, protesting the lack of on campus early voting sites at two big
schools, UNC Greensboro and North Carolina A&T University, which is the biggest HBCU in the
country. Shaya Rosier, a senior at North Carolina A&T, is the co-founder of Protect Ours NC,
an organization working to make voting more accessible for students. And I'm sure there's
other ones that are facing this, not just in North Carolina, but throughout the nation. So
I think right now we are all at a crossroads where we are deciding to stand up for what is
ours and, you know, demand what we need and then also begin to build what we deserve.
Rosier is speaking there to NPR's weekend edition. You're listening to NPR News.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says at least four service members were killed,
dozens of others injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta. The cause is under investigation,
but the Canadian military says there is no indication of terrorism. Meanwhile, advanced
polls closed late yesterday in Alberta ahead of tomorrow's referendum that may determine the
future map of Canada. As Dan Karpentjek reports, people in Alberta are deciding whether they want
to stay in Canada or start the process of separation. Rallies have ramped up over the
past week with the most recent taking place in front of the Alberta legislature in Edmonton.
It was a final push to rally this separatist cause. Hundreds of thousands of Albertans have
already voted in advanced polls or cast their mail-in ballots. Prime Minister Mark Carney,
who grew up in Alberta, attended forever Canadian rallies last week in Edmonton and Calgary,
urging people to vote in favor of Canada, saying, quote, "We are stronger together."
Albertans will vote on 10 referendum questions, the most notable whether to begin the process
of separation. If successful, that would mean another referendum, this one binding,
on whether they should go their own way as a country. Surveys have shown that most Albertans
want to stay in Canada, but a significant number back in dependence. For NPR News,
I'm Dan Karpentjek in Toronto. China says it plans to restrict or ban exports of 40
technologies including AI, chips and solar power for national security. This as its tech race with
countries including the U.S. intensifies that proposal includes 23 AI technologies.
